title: The House That Didn’t Ask
descriptions: Volume V cover. K rests his hands on a red guitar on Mike’s couch. Two mugs stand on the side table.
Iona and Mara record four peaks on their local receiver. On Earth, K listens as the line goes quiet.
K reaches for another repair at Waldo’s bench. Mike moves the tools aside and drives him home through the rain.
Mike offers K the couch for a bed. An old cassette stirs an image of a rehearsal.
A screwdriver and tape call up a musician, an ivory ceremonial mask, and a remembered cup of tea.
Mike offers a pillow as K tries to place the unfamiliar hallway and a remembered face.
Over coffee, K finds his hands already know how to work on Mike’s laptop.
A cassette player in Mike’s kitchen brings back the feeling of playing music with someone.
Mike and K test the foldout couch and its uncertain claim to be a bed.
A count-in comes back to K as his fingers tap the couch. Mike notices him keeping time.
Two speckled cups sit on the table. Mike taps twice; K adds the third tap on wood. In a crimson glimpse, Mike anticipates the guitar.
K chooses to rest. He can place himself in Mike’s living room even as the older images remain uncertain.
K tests the sticking strike plate. Mike offers him an ordinary glass of water.
A cutlery drawer opens onto a red memory of envelopes and cables. Mike distinguishes his own kitchen from K’s impressions.
A complicated remote and a blue television screen make both men laugh until K hears a familiar interval.
Iona’s drumsticks in a remembered rehearsal dissolve into a prison corridor. K steadies himself against the couch.
K records what he observed, what he remembers, and what he still cannot place. Mike sets his mug beside the laptop.
A faceless figure waits behind wet glass at midnight. K saves the fragment without giving it a person’s name.
Mike listens as K describes a drive across town and the feeling attached to it.
Iona and Mara open an agreed voice window from the Low Quarter. K asks about the fourth beat.
K asks Iona about the anger inside a song. They speak across the radio from their own rooms.
K hooks a wire at home. In a fragment, his scraped knuckles make the same hook on the recorder he built from shipboard scraps. He plucks a rough first note.
K begins a private guitar take. Rainy streets and a kitchen drawer hover inside the first verse.
A child’s hand reaches for a doorbell in K’s mind. Mike turns away so K can finish the chorus.
Folded shirts and old letters in a remembered drawer give way to the batteries beneath Mike’s television.
K looks at his scraped knuckles. Mike brings a towel for the spilled tea.
The kettle heats in Mike’s kitchen while an indistinct figure stands behind steam in the song.
A suitcase and sticky latch draw K to Mike’s front door. Mike carries a folded blanket.
The kitchen bulb goes dark. K has a screwdriver in hand before the conversation catches up.
Mike moves the remote, and K sets down the screwdriver. The two sit together through a silent panel before Mike makes a joke.
K finishes his take, stops the recording, and asks Mike to keep it private.
A ringing phone and dead bulb belong to the lyric. K turns his actual phone face down.
K names the rough take and marks the source unresolved. Mike tells him what to expect for breakfast.
Morning light reaches the couch. Mike brings two bowls of cereal past the broken kitchen fixture.
K saves the recording to a local drive and shuts the laptop. His bag has moved beside the couch.
In the Low Quarter, Iona finds an old local copy of the backing track and picks up her drumsticks.
Iona taps the rim, drops her boot, inhales, and comes in on the beat. Her voice takes its own rhythm over the shared instrumental.
A storm crosses the windshield. The page holds on Iona alone at the microphone as she asks if she was loved or was a place to hide.
A key on a counter and an empty car seat accompany Iona’s final lines. She saves her own local take.
During the next voice window, Mara plays Iona’s track into the radio. In Mike’s house, K recognizes the beat.
K listens through the static as his couch and a distant drum kit briefly overlap in his imagination.
Iona and K speak about the hurt their songs express. Each leaves the other’s recording in their own hands.
K accepts cereal from Mike while Iona returns to the drums. The broken kitchen light hangs above K’s quiet hands.
Because I Was Useful, lyric sheet one of two. K’s private rough demo, beginning with the midnight call.
Because I Was Useful, lyric sheet two of two. The bridge, final chorus, and the call about a kitchen light.
RIDE OR DIE, lyric sheet one of two. Iona’s vocal begins over the shared instrumental.
RIDE OR DIE, lyric sheet two of two. Iona sings about the spare key and setting down the phone.

Because I Was Useful
VERSE 1
She used to call at midnight, back when losing sleep felt youthful,
I’d drive across the city just to hear her call me beautiful.
I knew which bills were overdue, which kitchen drawers were too full,
She knew that I would always come; I knew how to be useful.
I told my friends she’d do the same; I wanted to sound truthful,
Then changed the subject when their smiles went quiet, small, and
rueful.
CHORUS
Not because she loved me, but because I was useful,
She said that I was all she had; I needed that to be truthful.
I gave her all my younger years so she could still feel youthful—
Not because she loved me, but because I was useful.
VERSE 2
The night I couldn’t leave my bed, her week was suddenly too full,
I said, “Of course, I understand,” and almost sounded truthful.
I asked her what she loved in me; she listed what was useful,
Then kissed the hands that fixed her world and told me they were
beautiful.
I kept my own grief folded; all her drawers were already too full,
And hated how I still felt hope whenever she looked rueful.

RIDE OR DIE
Under the weight of your beautiful lie,
Carrying memories, wondering why.
Reaching for someone who’s passing me by,
Swallowing everything, trying to fly.
Callously calling it “ride or die,”
Leaving me little but reasons to cry.
Gathering pieces you scattered, I try—
Finally letting your promises die.
You called us forever; I called it ride or die,
Held onto your promise while the years went by.
You slept through the thunder; I watched the sky,
Learned how to whisper so you wouldn’t hear me cry.

RIDE OR DIE
I made myself useful; you kept me nearby,
Fixed every fracture and never asked why.
You kissed me goodnight with your bags standing by,
I stared at the ceiling rehearsing goodbye.
Was I someone you loved or a place to hide?
A hand on the wheel when you needed a ride?
I swallowed the questions; they burned me inside,
You called it devotion whenever I complied.
Ride or die, ride or die,
I wore out my heart keeping yours supplied.
You wanted forever with an exit nearby,
I wanted the truth, even dressed as a lie.
Now your key’s on the counter; the morning is dry,
No rain on the window to help me deny.
I reach for the phone, then I set it aside—
For once, there is nobody here to satisfy.
